practicals.label: Activity 1.1
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate this activity and initiate discussion as per direction.
One student should measure the length of a writing board with his hand. The same should be repeated by four or five students. Are all the measurements same? If they differ, then why? What is the solution to avoid confusion?
In the early days people used to measure length using hand or arm, foot or steps. This measurement may result in confusion as the measurement of different people may differ from each other because of different sizes of their hands, arms or steps. To avoid such confusion, there is a need of a standard so that measurement by any person may result the same. This standard of measurement is known as a unit.
[FIGURE: Photograph of the International Prototype kilogram inside a glass enclosure; caption: “The International Prototype kilogram”]
A measurement consists of two parts, a number and a unit. A measurement without unit is meaningless.
Not very far in the past, every country in the world had its own units of measurements. However, problems were faced when people of different countries exchanged scientific information or traded with other countries using different units. Eventually, people got the idea of standardizing the units of measurements which could be used by all countries for efficient working and growth of mutual trade, business and share scientific information.
procedure: The teacher facilitates the activity and initiates discussion.
One student measures the length of the writing board with his hand.
Repeat the measurement with four or five students.
Compare the measurements and discuss whether they are all the same; if they differ, discuss why and how confusion can be avoided.
Discuss why a standard unit of measurement is needed.
practicals.aim: To measure a writing board using hand lengths and observe why a standard unit is needed.

viva.question: What are the two parts of a measurement?
viva.answer: A number and a unit.

viva.question: Why might students get different measurements using their hands?
viva.answer: Their hands may be different sizes.

viva.question: What is a unit?
viva.answer: A standard used to measure a physical quantity.

viva.question: Why is a standard unit needed?
viva.answer: It helps different people obtain measurements that can be compared without confusion.

viva.question: Is a measurement without a unit meaningful?
viva.answer: No. A measurement without a unit is meaningless.

practicals.title: Measuring a writing board with hand lengths
precautions: Place the hand carefully along the board, without gaps or overlaps between successive hand lengths.
Keep the hand flat and use the same method throughout each measurement.
Take care not to move or disturb the board while measuring.
Record each student's reading clearly.
practicals.result: The students’ measurements differ because their hands are of different sizes. A standard unit is needed so that measurements made by different people can be compared consistently.

practicals.label: Activity 1.2
practicals.bookText:
(The teacher should facilitate to perform this activity by making groups. Each group should place ten coins one above the other. Record their total height using a metre rule. Divide by 10.
What is the thickness of one coin?
Now find the thickness of one coin using Vernier Callipers.
What is the result?
Each group should comment on the measurement using the two instruments.
procedure: Work in groups.
Place ten coins one above the other.
Record their total height using a metre rule.
Divide the total height by 10 to find the thickness of one coin.
Find the thickness of one coin using Vernier callipers.
Compare the measurements made using the two instruments and comment on them.
practicals.aim: To determine the thickness of one coin using a metre rule and Vernier callipers.

viva.question: Why are ten coins placed one above the other?
viva.answer: Measuring the combined height reduces the effect of measurement uncertainty on one coin.

viva.question: How do you find the thickness of one coin from the stack measurement?
viva.answer: Divide the total height of the ten coins by 10.

viva.question: Which instrument can measure a coin’s thickness more precisely?
viva.answer: Vernier callipers.

viva.question: How should the coins be arranged for the metre-rule measurement?
viva.answer: They should be stacked flat and aligned directly above one another.

viva.question: What should you check before using Vernier callipers?
viva.answer: Check that the jaws close properly and that the instrument has no zero error.

calculation: Metre rule: thickness of 10 coins = 18 mm
Thickness of one coin = 18 mm ÷ 10 = 1.8 mm
Vernier callipers: thickness of one coin = 1.8 mm
practicals.diagram: Draw two labelled setups: ten coins stacked beside a metre rule, labelled “10 coins”, “metre rule” and “total height”; and one coin held between Vernier callipers, labelled “coin”, “fixed jaw”, “movable jaw” and “Vernier scale”.
practicals.title: Thickness of a coin
precautions: Stack the coins flat and align them carefully.
Keep the metre rule upright and read the height at eye level.
Hold the coin squarely between the Vernier-calliper jaws.
Close the jaws gently without pressing or squeezing the coin.
Check for zero error before taking a Vernier-calliper reading.
practicals.result: The thickness of one coin is 1.8 mm by both methods. The measurements agree for these readings.

practicals.label: Activity 1.3
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the activity by making groups and ask them to find the thickness of 100 sheets of a textbook using a micrometre screw gauge. Dividing this thickness by 100, estimate the thickness of one sheet.
FOR YOUR INFORMATION:
The most precise balance is the digital electronic balance. It can measure mass of the order of 0.1mg
procedure: Work in a group and take 100 sheets of a textbook.
Use a micrometre screw gauge to measure the combined thickness of the 100 sheets.
Repeat the measurement at a few positions and record the readings.
Find the average thickness of the 100 sheets.
Divide this thickness by 100 to estimate the thickness of one sheet.
practicals.aim: To estimate the thickness of one textbook sheet by measuring the combined thickness of 100 sheets with a micrometre screw gauge.

viva.question: Why do we measure 100 sheets instead of one sheet?
viva.answer: The combined thickness is easier to measure accurately; dividing by 100 gives the thickness of one sheet.

viva.question: Which instrument is used in this activity?
viva.answer: A micrometre screw gauge.

viva.question: What is the SI unit of length?
viva.answer: The metre (m).

viva.question: How do you find the thickness of one sheet?
viva.answer: Divide the measured thickness of 100 sheets by 100.

viva.question: Why should the screw gauge be tightened gently?
viva.answer: To avoid compressing or damaging the sheets and affecting the reading.

calculation: Mean thickness of 100 sheets = (8.02 mm + 8.00 mm + 8.01 mm) ÷ 3 = 8.01 mm
Thickness of one sheet = 8.01 mm ÷ 100 = 0.0801 mm
Thickness of one sheet = 0.0801 mm × 10⁻³ m/mm = 8.01 × 10⁻⁵ m
practicals.diagram: Draw a labelled micrometre screw gauge holding a stack of 100 textbook sheets between the anvil and spindle; label the frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve (main scale), thimble, ratchet, and sheets.
practicals.title: Thickness of one textbook sheet using a micrometre screw gauge
precautions: Make sure the 100 sheets are aligned evenly and are not folded.
Place the stack squarely between the anvil and spindle.
Tighten the screw gently using the ratchet; do not force it.
Take readings at a few positions and use their mean.
practicals.result: The estimated thickness of one textbook sheet is 0.0801 mm, or 8.01 × 10⁻⁵ m.

practicals.label: Activity 1.4
practicals.bookText: The teacher should help each group to make a paper scale having least count 0.2 cm and 0.5 cm.
procedure: Take a strip of paper and draw a straight line along its length.
Using a ruler, mark centimetre divisions along the line and label them 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on.
For the first scale, divide each centimetre into 5 equal parts and draw small marks at the divisions.
For the second scale, divide each centimetre into 2 equal parts and draw small marks at the divisions.
Label the scales to show their least counts.
practicals.aim: To make paper scales having least counts of 0.2 cm and 0.5 cm.

viva.question: What is the least count of an instrument?
viva.answer: It is the smallest measurement that the instrument can read.

viva.question: How many equal parts are there in 1 cm on the 0.2 cm scale?
viva.answer: Five equal parts.

viva.question: How many equal parts are there in 1 cm on the 0.5 cm scale?
viva.answer: Two equal parts.

viva.question: What is 0.2 cm in millimetres?
viva.answer: 2 mm.

viva.question: What is 0.5 cm in millimetres?
viva.answer: 5 mm.

calculation: For the first scale: least count = 1 cm ÷ 5 = 0.2 cm = 2 mm.
For the second scale: least count = 1 cm ÷ 2 = 0.5 cm = 5 mm.
practicals.diagram: Draw two straight paper scales, each marked in centimetres from 0 onwards; show each centimetre divided into five equal parts on the first scale and two equal parts on the second, and label them “Least count = 0.2 cm” and “Least count = 0.5 cm”.
practicals.title: Making paper scales of different least counts
precautions: Draw the scale line straight and keep the paper flat.
Make all subdivisions equal in length.
Use a sharp pencil to make fine, clear marks.
Label the centimetre marks and least counts clearly.
practicals.result: Two paper scales were made: one with a least count of 0.2 cm (2 mm) and the other with a least count of 0.5 cm (5 mm).

practicals.label: Activity 1.5
practicals.bookText:
Model of a sandclock
The teacher should arrange the required articles and help students to make a model of a sandclock as shown in the figure. Using two glass funnels, adhesive tape, two lids, and dry sand. Observe how much time it takes for the sand to flow down once completely. Make a paper scale from this and paste on the glass funnels along straight side.
[FIGURE Sandclock: Hourglass with sand in the upper and lower chambers. Caption: Sandclock.]
procedure: Arrange two glass funnels, adhesive tape, two lids, and dry sand.
Make a model of a sandclock using the two funnels and secure them with adhesive tape.
Put dry sand in the upper funnel and set the sandclock upright.
Start the stopwatch as the sand begins to flow.
At 5-second intervals, note the position of the sand surface along the straight side of the upper funnel and record the elapsed time and position.
Note the time when all the sand has flowed down completely.
Make a paper scale from the recorded sand-level observations and paste it along the straight side of the glass funnels.
practicals.aim: To make a model sandclock and use timed sand-level observations to prepare a paper time scale.

viva.question: What does a sandclock measure?
viva.answer: It measures a time interval.

viva.question: What makes the sand flow from one funnel to the other?
viva.answer: Gravity.

viva.question: Why should the sand be dry?
viva.answer: Dry sand flows more freely and consistently.

viva.question: What should you do when starting the timing?
viva.answer: Start the stopwatch as the sand begins to flow.

viva.question: What does each mark on the paper scale show?
viva.answer: The sand level corresponding to an elapsed time.

calculation: Time for complete flow = stopwatch reading when the upper funnel is empty = 20 s.

columns: Distance of sand surface from funnel junction along the upper funnel (cm)

practicals.diagram: Draw two glass funnels joined narrow-end to narrow-end with adhesive tape, showing sand in the upper funnel flowing into the lower funnel; label upper funnel, lower funnel, dry sand, direction of flow, adhesive tape, lids, paper time scale, and the scale’s straight-side position marks.
practicals.title: Model of a sandclock
precautions: Keep the sandclock upright and steady while the sand flows.
Start the stopwatch as soon as the sand begins to flow.
Record each sand-level position at the same 5-second intervals.
Use dry sand and ensure the passage between the funnels is not blocked.
Secure the funnels with tape and handle the glass carefully.
practicals.result: A paper time scale was prepared from the timed sand-level observations. In this trial, the sand flowed completely in 20 s.

practicals.label: Activity 1.6
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the groups to perform this activity following the given instructions.
1. Take a liquid in which the given solid does not dissolve.
2. Note the initial position of liquid surface.
3. Put the solid in the cylinder containing liquid.
4. Note again the position of liquid surface in the cylinder which rises due to solid.
5. The difference of the two readings is the volume of the solid.
[FIGURE: Two graduated cylinders; the initial liquid level in the left cylinder is labelled A, and the higher liquid level in the right cylinder, with a solid immersed in it, is labelled B.]
Caution: While taking a reading, keep your eye in front and in line with the lower meniscus of the water.
DO YOU KNOW?
Ancient Chinese used to estimate the volume of grains by sounding their containing vessels.
procedure: Take a liquid in which the given solid does not dissolve.
Note the initial position of liquid surface.
Put the solid in the cylinder containing liquid.
Note again the position of liquid surface in the cylinder which rises due to solid.
Find the volume of the solid by subtracting the initial reading from the final reading.
practicals.aim: To find the volume of a solid by measuring the rise in liquid level in a graduated cylinder.

viva.question: How is the volume of the solid found?
viva.answer: By subtracting the initial liquid reading from the reading after immersing the solid.

viva.question: Why must the liquid not dissolve the solid?
viva.answer: Dissolving would change the solid and make its volume measurement inaccurate.

viva.question: How should you position your eye when taking a reading?
viva.answer: Keep the eye in front and in line with the lower meniscus.

viva.question: What causes the liquid level to rise?
viva.answer: The immersed solid displaces liquid.

viva.question: What is the SI unit of volume?
viva.answer: The cubic metre (m³).

viva.question: How many cubic centimetres are in one millilitre?
viva.answer: One millilitre equals one cubic centimetre.

calculation: Trial 1: Volume = 58 mL − 40 mL = 18 mL
Trial 2: Volume = 68 mL − 50 mL = 18 mL
Trial 3: Volume = 78 mL − 60 mL = 18 mL
Mean volume = (18 + 18 + 18) mL ÷ 3 = 18 mL
Volume = 18 cm³
apparatus: Liquid in which the solid does not dissolve
practicals.diagram: Draw two graduated cylinders: label the initial liquid level A in the first cylinder; in the second, draw the solid immersed in liquid and label the higher liquid level B, and label both cylinders and the liquid.
practicals.title: Volume of a solid by liquid displacement
precautions: Use a liquid in which the solid does not dissolve.
Keep your eye in front and in line with the lower meniscus while taking each reading.
Put the solid gently into the cylinder to avoid splashing liquid.
Ensure the solid is completely immersed and has no air bubbles attached to it.
practicals.result: The volume of the solid is 18 mL, or 18 cm³.

practicals.label: Activity 1.7
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the groups to take a metallic ball or a pendulum bob. Measure its diameter and then volume by placing it in between two wooden blocks alongside a ruler. Then use measuring cylinder and comment on the result of this two onset activities.
[FIGURE: A metallic ball placed between two wooden blocks beside a ruler marked 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.]
practicals.title: Volume of a metallic ball
practicals.aim: To measure the diameter and volume of a metallic ball using wooden blocks, a ruler, and a measuring cylinder, and compare the volume measurements.

practicals.label: Activity 4.1
practicals.bookText:
Take your class to play ground where a see-saw is available. Let a lighter child sits on the left side and the heavier one on the right side of the see-saw. The distances of both the children from the pivot should be equal. The force exerted by each child is equal to his weight acting downward. Does the heavier child move down? Yes, because he is exerting larger force. Now move the heavier child nearer to the pivot and the lighter child away from the pivot as shown in the figure. Ask the students what do they observe?
[FIGURE: A see-saw with a lighter child on the left and a heavier child on the right, with a central pivot and arrows showing moment arms on both sides. Labels: Pivot, Moment arm, Moment arm.]
You will see that the see-saw tilts to the opposite direction and the lighter child moves down. This shows that the turning effect of a force does not depend only on its magnitude but also on the location where it acts. Therefore, we can say that the greater the force, the greater is its turning effect. Moreover, the larger the perpendicular distance of the force from the axis of rotation, the greater is its turning effect.
The line along which the force acts is called the line of action of the force.
The perpendicular distance of the line of action of a force from the axis of rotation is known as moment arm of the force or simply moment arm.
The moment arms of both the children are shown in the figure of activity 4.1. There are many other examples to observe the turning or rotational effect of a force. It is harder to open a door by pushing it at a point closer to the
hinge as compared to push it at the handle (Fig. 4.4). That is why, door or window handles are always installed at larger distances from hinges to produce larger moment of force by applying less force. This makes the doors be opened or closed more easier. Similarly, it requires greater force to open a nut by a spanner if you hold it closer such as point A than point B (Fig. 4.5).
[FIGURE Fig. 4.4: A door with a handle.]
[FIGURE Fig. 4.5: A spanner holding a nut; upward force F is applied at point A, and upward force F′ at point B. Labels: Nut, A, B.]
procedure: Take the class to a playground where a see-saw is available.
Let a lighter child sit on the left side and a heavier child on the right side of the see-saw, at equal distances from the pivot.
Observe whether the heavier child moves down.
Move the heavier child nearer to the pivot and the lighter child farther from it.
Adjust their positions enough that the lighter child’s weight multiplied by its moment arm is greater than the heavier child’s weight multiplied by its moment arm.
Observe that the see-saw tilts to the opposite direction and the lighter child moves down.
practicals.aim: To observe how the magnitude of a force and its moment arm affect its turning effect.

viva.question: What is the turning effect of a force called?
viva.answer: Moment of force, or torque.

viva.question: What is a moment arm?
viva.answer: The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.

viva.question: What is the line of action of a force?
viva.answer: The line along which the force acts.

viva.question: How is the moment of force calculated?
viva.answer: Moment of force = force × perpendicular moment arm.

viva.question: Why does the heavier child move down when both children sit equally far from the pivot?
viva.answer: The heavier child exerts a greater weight, so has the greater turning effect.

viva.question: When can the lighter child move down after the children change positions?
viva.answer: When the lighter child’s weight multiplied by its moment arm exceeds the heavier child’s corresponding product.

practicals.diagram: Draw a see-saw with a lighter child on the left and a heavier child on the right, a central pivot, downward weight arrows, and perpendicular moment arms on both sides; label the Pivot and each Moment arm.
practicals.title: Turning Effect of Force on a See-saw
precautions: Use the see-saw only with adult or teacher supervision.
Sit properly and hold the handles, if provided.
Do not stand, jump, or lean suddenly on the see-saw.
Change positions gradually and keep the area around the see-saw clear.
practicals.result: The turning effect of a force depends on both the force and its moment arm. The lighter child moves down only when the lighter child’s weight multiplied by its moment arm exceeds the heavier child’s corresponding product.

practicals.label: Activity 4.2
practicals.bookText:
Balance a metre rule on a wedge at its centre of gravity such that the metre rule stays horizontal. Suspend two weights w_1 and w_2 on one side of the metre rule at distance l_1 and l_2 from the centre and a third weight w_3 on the other side at distance l_3 until the rule is again balanced.
[FIGURE: A horizontal metre rule supported at CG on a wedge, with weights w_1 and w_2 hanging to the left and weight w_3 hanging to the right. The distances are labelled l_1 from w_1 to CG, l_2 from w_2 to CG and l_3 from CG to w_3.]
The weights w_1 and w_2 tend to rotate the rod anticlockwise about CG and the weight w_3 tends to rotate it clockwise. The values of the moments of the weights are w_1 × l_1, w_2 × l_2 and w_3 × l_3. When the metre rule is balanced, then
Total anticlockwise moments = Total clockwise moments
w_1 × l_1 + w_2 × l_2 = w_3 × l_3 ........................(4.6)
This is known as principle of moments, which is stated as:
When a body is in balanced position, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.
procedure: Balance a metre rule on a wedge at its centre of gravity such that the metre rule stays horizontal.
Suspend two weights w₁ and w₂ on one side of the metre rule at distances l₁ and l₂ from the centre, and a third weight w₃ on the other side at distance l₃.
Adjust the positions of the weights until the rule is again balanced.
Record the weights and their distances from the centre of gravity.
Calculate the moments and compare the total anticlockwise moments with the total clockwise moment.
practicals.aim: To verify the principle of moments using a balanced metre rule.

viva.question: What is the moment of a force?
viva.answer: The product of the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot.

viva.question: What is the SI unit of moment?
viva.answer: The newton metre (N m).

viva.question: What is the pivot in this activity?
viva.answer: The wedge supporting the metre rule at its centre of gravity.

viva.question: Which way do w₁ and w₂ tend to turn the rule?
viva.answer: Anticlockwise.

viva.question: State the principle of moments.
viva.answer: For a balanced body, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.

calculation: Trial 1: Anticlockwise moment = (0.20 N × 0.30 m) + (0.30 N × 0.20 m) = 0.12 N m.
Trial 1: Clockwise moment = 0.60 N × 0.20 m = 0.12 N m.
Trial 2: Anticlockwise moment = (0.30 N × 0.30 m) + (0.20 N × 0.15 m) = 0.12 N m.
Trial 2: Clockwise moment = 0.40 N × 0.30 m = 0.12 N m.
Trial 3: Anticlockwise moment = (0.20 N × 0.25 m) + (0.40 N × 0.20 m) = 0.13 N m.
Trial 3: Clockwise moment = 0.65 N × 0.20 m = 0.13 N m.
practicals.diagram: Draw a horizontal metre rule supported on a wedge at CG; show w₁ and w₂ hanging to the left and w₃ hanging to the right, and label the distances l₁ from w₁ to CG, l₂ from w₂ to CG, and l₃ from CG to w₃.
practicals.title: Principle of Moments
precautions: Place the wedge at the metre rule’s centre of gravity.
Make sure the metre rule is horizontal before taking readings.
Measure each distance from the centre of gravity to the line of action of the weight.
Hang the weights freely and ensure they do not touch the table or one another.
Take readings only after the rule has come to rest.
practicals.result: The sum of the anticlockwise moments is equal to the sum of the clockwise moments when the metre rule is balanced. The principle of moments is verified.

practicals.label: Activity 6.1
practicals.bookText:
The teacher will arrange a helical spring with an attached pointer, slotted weights, half metre rule or scale, iron stand and will facilitate to perform this activity as per instructions. Note that a spring of helical or spiral shape is called helical spring. Its length should be greater than its diameter.
(i) Suspend a helical spring with the stand.
(ii) Adjust the pointer so that it does not touch the scale but can move up and down freely along the scale.
(iii) Place a slotted weight say 50 g in the hanger and note the position of pointer on the scale.
(iv) Repeat this step for five times, each time increasing the load in equal amount.
(v) Draw a graph between force F along y-axis and extension x along x-axis.
(vi) What is the shape of the graph?
(vii) What does it show?
(viii) Find the slope of the straight line. What does it represent?
[FIGURE: A helical spring suspended from a stand beside a vertical scale, with a pointer and a weight hanging from the spring.]
Quick Quiz
1. If the above experiment is repeated with a stiffer spring (high value of k), what will be the effect on the graph?
2. How can you find the value of unknown weight using this experiment?
procedure: Suspend a helical spring from the iron stand beside the vertical scale.
Adjust the pointer so that it does not touch the scale but can move up and down freely along it.
Note the pointer position with no load to use as the initial position.
Place a 50 g slotted weight in the hanger and note the pointer position on the scale.
Repeat the loading step, increasing the load by 50 g each time, and note the pointer position for each load.
Find the extension for each load by subtracting the initial pointer position from the loaded pointer position.
Calculate the force for each load using F = mg.
Draw a graph between force F along the y-axis and extension x along the x-axis.
Observe the shape of the graph and find the slope of the straight line.
practicals.aim: To investigate the relationship between the force applied to a helical spring and its extension.

viva.question: What is a helical spring?
viva.answer: A spring of helical or spiral shape is called a helical spring.

viva.question: What is the shape of the force-extension graph?
viva.answer: It is a straight line through the origin, while the spring remains within its elastic limit.

viva.question: What does the straight-line graph show?
viva.answer: It shows that force is directly proportional to extension.

viva.question: What does the slope of the force-extension graph represent?
viva.answer: It represents the spring constant, k, in N/m.

viva.question: What happens to the graph for a stiffer spring with a higher k?
viva.answer: Its slope is greater, so a greater force is needed for the same extension.

viva.question: How can an unknown weight be found using this experiment?
viva.answer: Measure its extension, find its force from F = kx, then find its mass using m = F/g.

calculation: For a 50 g load: m = 0.050 kg.
Force, F = mg = 0.050 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 0.49 N.
Using the readings, the extension for each load is the loaded pointer position minus the initial pointer position.
practicals.diagram: Draw a helical spring suspended from a labelled iron stand, with a pointer beside a vertical scale and a hanger carrying slotted weights; label the spring, pointer, scale, stand, hanger and slotted weights.
practicals.title: Force and extension of a helical spring
precautions: Keep the pointer close to, but not touching, the scale.
Read the pointer at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Add the weights gently and wait for the spring to stop oscillating before taking a reading.
Increase the load by equal amounts and do not load the spring beyond its elastic limit.
practicals.result: The force-extension graph is a straight line, showing that force is directly proportional to extension within the elastic limit. The spring constant from the sample readings is 49 N/m.

practicals.label: Activity 6.2
practicals.bookText:
Teacher should facilitate to help the groups to pour some water in a measuring cylinder. If the substance is soluble in water, then use a liquid in which the substance is insoluble. Note the level of the liquid in the cylinder. Now gently drop the substance into the cylinder. The rise in the level gives the volume of the substance.
[FIGURE: A measuring cylinder containing liquid and a solid at the bottom, with marks showing the liquid level.]
procedure: Pour some water into a measuring cylinder.
If the substance is soluble in water, use a liquid in which the substance is insoluble.
Note the level of the liquid in the cylinder.
Gently drop the substance into the cylinder.
Note the new level. The rise in the level gives the volume of the substance.
Repeat the measurement to obtain further readings.
practicals.aim: To find the volume of a solid by measuring the rise in liquid level in a measuring cylinder.

viva.question: How is the volume of the solid found?
viva.answer: Subtract the initial liquid level from the final level.

viva.question: Why does the liquid level rise when the solid is dropped in?
viva.answer: The solid displaces liquid equal to its volume.

viva.question: What should you do if the solid dissolves in water?
viva.answer: Use a liquid in which the solid is insoluble.

viva.question: What is the SI unit of volume?
viva.answer: The cubic metre (m³).

viva.question: What is the relation between 1 mL and 1 cm³?
viva.answer: 1 mL = 1 cm³.

calculation: Trial 1: Volume of solid = 40 mL − 30 mL = 10 mL = 10 cm³.
Trial 2: Volume of solid = 36 mL − 25 mL = 11 mL = 11 cm³.
Trial 3: Volume of solid = 49 mL − 40 mL = 9 mL = 9 cm³.
Mean volume = (10 cm³ + 11 cm³ + 9 cm³) ÷ 3 = 10 cm³.
apparatus: Water (or another liquid in which the substance is insoluble)
practicals.diagram: Draw a labelled measuring cylinder containing liquid and a solid at the bottom; show and label the initial liquid level, the final liquid level, the solid, and the measuring-cylinder scale.
practicals.title: Volume of a solid by liquid displacement
precautions: Use a liquid in which the solid is insoluble.
Drop the solid gently into the cylinder to avoid splashing.
Keep the measuring cylinder upright on a level surface.
Read the liquid level at eye level.
Ensure the solid is fully immersed and that no air bubbles cling to it.
practicals.result: The volume of the solid, found from the rise in liquid level, is 10 cm³.

practicals.label: Activity 6.3
practicals.bookText:
Teacher should help the students to perform this activity and initiate discussion as per instructions:
i. Make three small holes at different heights in the side of a container as shown in the figure.
ii. Fill the container with water.
iii. Observe the water streams flowing out of the holes. It is initially normal to the surface.
iv. Which one of the streams hits the ground at larger distance?
v. At which position the liquid has more pressure?
[FIGURE: A container of water with three holes at different heights; streams of water flow out and curve down at different distances. Labels: “LOWEST PRESSURE”, “WATER”, “HIGHEST PRESSURE”.]
You will observe that the stream from each hole, initially flows out normal to the surface before curving down due to gravity and the lowest hole has more pressure. It shows that liquid pressure increases with depth.
procedure: Make three small holes at different heights in the side of a container.
Fill the container with water.
Observe the water streams flowing out of the holes; each stream initially flows out normal to the surface.
Observe which stream hits the ground at the larger distance.
Discuss at which position the liquid has more pressure.
practicals.aim: To observe how liquid pressure changes with depth.

viva.question: In which direction does water initially flow out of a hole in the side of the container?
viva.answer: Normal (perpendicular) to the surface.

viva.question: Which hole has the greatest liquid pressure?
viva.answer: The lowest hole, because it is at the greatest depth below the water surface.

viva.question: How does liquid pressure change with depth?
viva.answer: Liquid pressure increases with depth.

viva.question: Why do the water streams curve downwards?
viva.answer: Gravity pulls the water downwards.

viva.question: Does the stream from the lowest hole always hit the ground farthest away?
viva.answer: No. The horizontal distance depends on both the hole’s depth below the water surface and its height above the ground, so a middle stream may travel farthest.

apparatus: Pin or nail to make the holes
practicals.diagram: Draw a container partly filled with water, with three holes at different heights and curved water streams from them; label the water, the top hole “LOWEST PRESSURE”, and the lowest hole “HIGHEST PRESSURE”.
practicals.title: Pressure in liquids
precautions: Make the three holes small and at clearly different heights.
Keep the container upright and steady while observing.
Fill the container carefully to avoid spilling water.
Keep the area around the container clear and dry to prevent slipping.
practicals.result: The lowest hole has the greatest pressure because liquid pressure increases with depth. The stream that travels farthest depends on both the hole’s depth below the water surface and its height above the ground.

practicals.label: Activity 6.4
practicals.bookText:
Teacher should demonstrate or help the students to perform by following the instructions given below:
(i) Fill a polythene shopping bag with water.
(ii) Poke several holes by using a pin on the bag.
(iii) Squeeze the bag gently.
(iv) What do you observe?
Squeezing the top of bag causes the water to squirt on in all directions. It means the pressure is transmitted equally throughout the liquid.
[FIGURE: A person squeezes a polythene bag containing water above a container while another person points toward the bag.]
procedure: Fill a polythene shopping bag with water.
Poke several holes in the bag using a pin.
Squeeze the bag gently.
Observe the directions in which the water squirts from the holes.
practicals.aim: To observe how pressure is transmitted through a liquid.

viva.question: What happens when the bag is squeezed?
viva.answer: Water squirts out through the holes in different directions.

viva.question: What does this activity show about pressure in a liquid?
viva.answer: Pressure is transmitted throughout the liquid.

viva.question: In what directions does the water squirt?
viva.answer: It squirts in different directions.

viva.question: Why should the bag be squeezed gently?
viva.answer: To observe the flow safely and avoid bursting the bag.

practicals.diagram: Draw a water-filled polythene bag with several holes, hands gently squeezing it, water jets coming out in different directions, and a container below; label the bag, water, holes, hands, water jets, and container.
practicals.title: Pressure transmission in a liquid
precautions: Use the pin carefully and keep its point away from fingers.
Make several small holes rather than large ones.
Squeeze the bag gently.
Keep the container below the bag to catch the water.
practicals.result: When the bag is squeezed, water squirts out through its holes in different directions. This shows that pressure is transmitted throughout the liquid.

practicals.label: Activity 6.5
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should perform this activity in the class following the given instructions.
Boil some water in a tin can. When it is full of steam, remove it from the burner and close its mouth by an air tight cork. Then pour cold water over it. The can crumples as shown in the figure. Why does the tin crumples?
[FIGURE: An upright tin can on a stand over a burner, and a hand pouring water onto a crumpled tin can.]
procedure: The teacher boils some water in a tin can.
When the can is full of steam, the teacher removes it from the burner and closes its mouth with an airtight cork.
The teacher pours cold water over the can.
Observe the can as it crumples.
practicals.aim: To demonstrate the effect of atmospheric pressure when steam inside a tin can condenses.

viva.question: What causes the can to crumple?
viva.answer: Atmospheric pressure pushes the can inward when the pressure inside it becomes lower.

viva.question: What happens to the steam when cold water is poured over the can?
viva.answer: The steam condenses into liquid water.

viva.question: Why does condensation lower the pressure inside the can?
viva.answer: Condensation greatly reduces the amount of water vapour exerting pressure inside the can.

viva.question: In which direction does atmospheric pressure act?
viva.answer: It acts in all directions.

viva.question: Why must the cork be airtight?
viva.answer: It prevents air from entering the can and equalising the pressure.

practicals.diagram: Draw the two stages: an upright tin can on a stand over a burner, and a crumpled tin can with a hand pouring cold water over it; label the tin can, stand, burner, airtight cork, cold water and crumpled can.
practicals.title: Crumpling of a tin can by atmospheric pressure
precautions: The teacher should perform this activity.
Keep hands and face away from the hot can and burner.
Use suitable heat-resistant protection when handling the hot can.
Make sure the cork fits airtight before pouring cold water.
Keep the burner on a stable, heat-resistant surface.
practicals.result: The can crumples because the steam inside condenses, lowering the pressure within it. The greater atmospheric pressure outside pushes the can inward.

practicals.label: Activity 6.6
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the groups to follow the instructions given below.
i. Fill a syringe with water and insert its nozzle into a thin plastic tube.
ii. Press the syringe to fill the tube with water.
iii. Half fill the second syringe with water and insert its nozzle to the other end of the tube.
iv. Press one plunger in through some distance.
v. Is the second plunger pushed out through the same distance?
vi. Is the pressure transmitted to the second plunger by the liquid?
vii. What is your inference?
[FIGURE: Two syringes connected by a plastic tube containing water; the left plunger is moving out and the right plunger is pressed in. Labels: “Plunger moving out”, “Water”, “Plastic tube”, “Plunger pressed in”.]
procedure: Fill a syringe with water and insert its nozzle into a thin plastic tube.
Press the syringe to fill the tube with water.
Half fill the second syringe with water and insert its nozzle to the other end of the tube.
Press one plunger in through some distance.
Observe whether the second plunger is pushed out through the same distance.
Observe whether the pressure is transmitted to the second plunger by the liquid.
State your inference.
practicals.aim: To demonstrate that pressure applied to a liquid is transmitted through the liquid to another plunger.

viva.question: What does Pascal’s law state?
viva.answer: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.

viva.question: What transmits the pressure from one syringe to the other?
viva.answer: The water in the connected tube and syringes.

viva.question: What happens when one plunger is pressed in?
viva.answer: The pressure transmitted through the water pushes the other plunger out.

viva.question: Why should the tube and syringes be filled with water?
viva.answer: So the applied pressure is transmitted through the liquid.

viva.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?
viva.answer: The pascal (Pa).

practicals.diagram: Draw two syringes connected by a water-filled plastic tube; label the plunger moving out, water, plastic tube, and plunger pressed in.
practicals.title: Demonstration of Pascal’s Law
precautions: Push the syringe plunger gently.
Make sure the tube is fitted securely to both syringe nozzles.
Fill the tube with water before connecting the second syringe.
Keep the apparatus steady while pressing a plunger.
practicals.result: Pressing one plunger transmits pressure through the water and pushes the other plunger out. This demonstrates Pascal’s law.

practicals.label: Activity 7.1
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should arrange hot water in some tea cups, thermometers and metal spoons. Make groups of the students. Each group will put the spoon in the hot water and stir it. Ask them what do they feel. Does the other end of the spoon also become hot?
Do they observe that the spoon also gets hotter? It means heat is being transferred from the hot water to the spoon because the temperature of the water was higher than that of the spoon.
Thus
Temperature can be defined as a physical quantity which determines the direction of flow of thermal energy.
This means that thermal energy is transferred from one object to another due to temperature difference of the two bodies. Therefore, we can define heat as follows:
Heat is the energy which is transferred from one object to another due to difference of temperature between the two bodies.
procedure: Arrange hot water in tea cups, thermometers and metal spoons.
Make groups of students.
Put a metal spoon in the hot water and stir it.
Observe what you feel and whether the other end of the spoon also becomes hot.
practicals.aim: To observe heat transfer from hot water to a metal spoon due to a difference in temperature.

viva.question: What is temperature?
viva.answer: Temperature is a physical quantity that determines the direction of flow of thermal energy.

viva.question: What is heat?
viva.answer: Heat is energy transferred from one object to another due to a temperature difference.

viva.question: In which direction does heat flow?
viva.answer: Heat flows from the object at higher temperature to the object at lower temperature.

viva.question: Why does the spoon become hotter?
viva.answer: Thermal energy transfers from the hotter water to the cooler spoon.

viva.question: Does the other end of the spoon also become hot?
viva.answer: Yes, heat travels through the metal spoon and warms its other end.

practicals.diagram: Draw a tea cup containing hot water with a metal spoon partly immersed and a thermometer in the water; label the tea cup, hot water, metal spoon, immersed end, other end and thermometer.
practicals.title: Heat transfer from hot water to a metal spoon
precautions: Handle the hot water and cup carefully to avoid burns or spills.
Do not touch the hot water or the immersed end of the spoon.
Hold the spoon by its handle and avoid touching the other end if it becomes hot.
Keep the thermometer secure and handle it carefully.
practicals.result: The spoon becomes hotter because thermal energy transfers from the hotter water to the cooler spoon. Heat flows from a higher-temperature object to a lower-temperature object.

practicals.label: Activity 8.1
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should divide the students into groups and provide them permanent magnets to perform this activity.
Each group should collect some items made of different materials such as copper wire, nickel ring, glass bottle, paper clips, iron nail, eraser, wooden ruler, plastic comb, etc. Place them on a table as shown in figure. Bring the permanent magnet close to each item one by one and observe which items are attracted by the magnet and which are not. Make a list of magnetic and non magnetic materials.
[FIGURE: A tabletop with assorted objects, including a ruler, clips, wire, and other small items.]
Materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt will be attracted by the magnet. They are magnetic materials. The materials such as brass, copper, wood, glass and plastic are not attracted by the magnet. They are called non-magnetic materials.
We will discuss different types of materials in detail later in this chapter.
FOR YOUR INFORMATION:
Over 1000 years ago, the Greeks discovered a rock called lodestone or magnetite that could attract materials that contained iron. Also, if suspended from a string to rotate freely, it would always settle in north-south direction. This unique property led to form the basis of compass which was later on used for navigation on land and at sea.
[FIGURE: A rock.]
procedure: Collect some items made of different materials, such as copper wire, nickel ring, glass bottle, paper clips, iron nail, eraser, wooden ruler and plastic comb.
Place the items on a table.
Bring the permanent magnet close to each item one by one.
Observe which items are attracted by the magnet and which are not.
Make a list of magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
practicals.aim: To identify magnetic and non-magnetic materials by testing them with a permanent magnet.

viva.question: What is a magnetic material?
viva.answer: A material that is attracted by a magnet.

viva.question: Name three magnetic materials.
viva.answer: Iron, nickel and cobalt.

viva.question: Is copper attracted by a magnet?
viva.answer: No, copper is non-magnetic.

viva.question: What is a non-magnetic material?
viva.answer: A material that is not attracted by a magnet.

viva.question: Is a paper clip usually magnetic?
viva.answer: Yes, paper clips are usually made of steel and are attracted by a magnet.

apparatus: Items made of different materials (for example, copper wire, nickel ring, glass bottle, paper clips, iron nail, eraser, wooden ruler and plastic comb)
practicals.diagram: Draw a tabletop with a permanent magnet being brought near assorted items; label the table, permanent magnet, iron nail, paper clip, copper wire, glass bottle, wooden ruler and plastic comb.
practicals.title: Identifying Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
precautions: Bring the magnet close to one item at a time.
Keep the items separated so they do not touch or attract one another.
Do not let the magnet strike or damage delicate items.
Keep the magnet away from electronic devices and magnetic cards.
practicals.result: The iron nail, nickel ring and paper clip are magnetic materials. The copper wire and glass bottle are non-magnetic materials.

practicals.label: Activity 8.2
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate each group to perform this activity as per instructions.
1. Place some iron filings scattered on the top of a card paper or a sheet of glass.
2. Move a magnet beneath the card paper, glass or a plastic sheet as shown in the figure.
3. What do you observe? Describe briefly.
[FIGURE: (a) Scattered Iron filings on a glass sheet. (b) Iron filings attracted by magnet; iron filings gather above a magnet held beneath the sheet.]
You must have seen the iron filings following the movement of the magnet. Magnetic force accounts for these movements. This activity also shows that magnets can attract objects containing iron, etc. even if they are not in direct contact with them.
procedure: Scatter some iron filings on top of a card paper, a sheet of glass, or a plastic sheet.
Move a magnet beneath the sheet.
Observe the movement of the iron filings and describe what happens.
practicals.aim: To observe the effect of a magnet on iron filings through a sheet.

viva.question: What happens to the iron filings when the magnet is moved beneath the sheet?
viva.answer: The filings are attracted and follow the movement of the magnet.

viva.question: Why do the iron filings move?
viva.answer: The magnet exerts a magnetic force on them.

viva.question: Do the magnet and iron filings need to touch for attraction to occur?
viva.answer: No, magnetic force can act without direct contact.

viva.question: What material in the filings is attracted by the magnet?
viva.answer: Iron.

apparatus: Card paper, a sheet of glass, or a plastic sheet
practicals.diagram: Draw iron filings scattered on a sheet in one sketch and gathered above a magnet held beneath the sheet in another; label the iron filings, sheet, magnet, and direction of magnet movement.
practicals.title: Attraction of Iron Filings by a Magnet
precautions: Keep the magnet beneath the sheet and do not let it touch the iron filings.
Move the magnet slowly so the filings can be observed clearly.
Keep iron filings away from the eyes and avoid inhaling them.
Collect the iron filings carefully after the activity.
practicals.result: The iron filings are attracted to the magnet and follow its movement, even though the magnet is not in direct contact with them.

practicals.label: Activity 8.3
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate each group to perform this activity as per instructions.
1. Take a magnetic compass. Put it on a table and see which end of its needle points north. The N-pole of the needle is usually coloured red.
2. Place a bar magnet on the table. Bring the compass near to its N-pole. In which direction does the N-pole of the needle stay?
[FIGURE: A bar magnet with N at its red left end and S at its blue right end, with a compass on either side. The compass dials show N, E, S and W.]
3. Put the compass near to the S-pole of the bar magnet. In which direction does the N-pole of the needle stay this time?
4. Now place an iron nail having its head in contact with any pole of the bar magnet.
[FIGURE: A bar magnet with N at the red left end and S at the blue right end, touching an iron nail. The nail is labelled N at the end near the magnet and S at its pointed end; a compass is beside the pointed end. The compass dial shows N, E, S and W.]
5. Put the compass near to the pointed end of an iron nail. Observe the direction in which N-pole of the needle settles. Has the nail become a magnet? Has magnetism been induced in it?
6. Take the bar magnet away from the nail. Again check the behaviour of the nail by bringing compass near to its ends. Does the magnetism vanish?
From the above activity, we conclude that the S-pole of the true magnet induces N-pole in the near end of the piece of iron (nail) while the far end of the iron piece becomes S-pole as shown in the figure.
It should be noted that the induced magnetism vanishes as the true magnet is removed.
procedure: Take a magnetic compass. Put it on a table and see which end of its needle points north. The N-pole of the needle is usually coloured red.
Place a bar magnet on the table. Bring the compass near to its N-pole. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays.
Put the compass near to the S-pole of the bar magnet. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays this time.
Place the head of an iron nail in contact with the S-pole of the bar magnet.

Put the compass near to the pointed end of the iron nail. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle settles. Note whether the nail has become a magnet and whether magnetism has been induced in it.
Take the bar magnet away from the nail. Again check the behaviour of the nail by bringing the compass near to its ends. Observe whether the magnetism vanishes.
practicals.aim: To observe the direction of a compass needle near a bar magnet and demonstrate induced magnetism in an iron nail.

viva.question: Which end of a compass needle points north?
viva.answer: The N-pole of the needle.

viva.question: What happens to the compass N-pole near the bar magnet’s N-pole?
viva.answer: It points away from the magnet’s N-pole.

viva.question: What happens to the compass N-pole near the bar magnet’s S-pole?
viva.answer: It points towards the magnet’s S-pole.

viva.question: Which pole is induced at the nail’s head when it touches the magnet’s S-pole?
viva.answer: An N-pole is induced at the nail’s head.

viva.question: Which pole is induced at the nail’s pointed end?
viva.answer: An S-pole is induced at the pointed end.

viva.question: What happens to the nail’s induced magnetism when the bar magnet is removed?
viva.answer: It vanishes.

rows: Near nail’s pointed end while its head touches the magnet’s S-pole
Pointed end acts as an S-pole
Near the nail after removing the bar magnet
No clear attraction to either end

practicals.diagram: Draw two labelled sketches: a bar magnet with N and S poles and a compass near each pole, showing the compass N-pole pointing away from N and towards S; then draw the magnet’s S-pole touching the nail’s head, label the nail end at the head N and its pointed end S, and show a nearby compass with its N-pole pointing towards the nail’s pointed end.
practicals.title: Induced magnetism in an iron nail
precautions: Keep the compass on a level table and allow its needle to settle before observing.
Keep the compass close to the magnet or nail, but do not let it touch them.
Ensure that the nail’s head remains in contact with the magnet’s S-pole during the observation.
Keep other magnets and magnetic objects away from the compass during the activity.
practicals.result: The S-pole of the bar magnet induces an N-pole at the nail’s head and an S-pole at its pointed end. The nail’s induced magnetism vanishes when the bar magnet is removed.

practicals.label: Activity 8.4
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the groups to provide each a bar magnet, a stand with clamp, some small nails made of iron and also some nails of steel. He should further supervise them to perform the activity as per instructions.
[FIGURE: A bar magnet clamped horizontally on a stand, with S at the left end and N at the right end. Chains of nails hang from both ends of the magnet.]
1. Clamp the bar magnet horizontally on the stand.
2. Touch the head of an iron nail to anyone end of the magnet. It will be attracted and stick to the magnet. Touch another iron nail to the lower end of the first one, does it stick to it?
Yes, it will, because the upper nail has become a magnet itself. Go on hanging iron nail one by one to make a chain until no more nails stay attached to the chain.
3. Try to hang steel nails at the other end of the bar magnet to form a similar chain.
4. Remove the chain of iron nails by pulling the topmost nail. Does the chain collapse?
5. Remove the chain of steel nails in the same way. Does this collapse?
You will observe that the chain of iron nails immediately collapses but the steel nails remain attached to each other for some time. This shows that the magnetism induced in the iron nails is temporary while that in the steel nails is permanent.
procedure: Clamp the bar magnet horizontally on the stand.
Touch the head of an iron nail to one end of the magnet. Touch another iron nail to the lower end of the first one and observe whether it sticks.
Go on hanging iron nails one by one to make a chain until no more nails stay attached to the chain.
Try to hang steel nails at the other end of the bar magnet to form a similar chain.
Remove the chain of iron nails by pulling the topmost nail. Observe whether the chain collapses.
Remove the chain of steel nails in the same way. Observe whether it collapses.
practicals.aim: To compare the temporary magnetism induced in iron nails with the permanent magnetism induced in steel nails.

viva.question: What happens when an iron nail touches a bar magnet?
viva.answer: It is attracted and becomes temporarily magnetised.

viva.question: Why can one iron nail hold another?
viva.answer: The first nail becomes a temporary magnet by induction.

viva.question: What happens to the chain of iron nails when the top nail is removed?
viva.answer: The chain immediately collapses.

viva.question: What happens to the chain of steel nails when the top nail is removed?
viva.answer: The nails remain attached to each other for some time.

viva.question: Which material shows temporary induced magnetism in this activity?
viva.answer: Iron.

viva.question: Which material retains magnetism for longer?
viva.answer: Steel.

rows: Nails remain attached for some time

practicals.diagram: Draw a bar magnet clamped horizontally on a stand, labelled S at the left end and N at the right end, with chains of nails hanging from both ends; label the bar magnet, stand, clamp, iron-nail chain, and steel-nail chain.
practicals.title: Temporary and permanent magnetism in nails
precautions: Clamp the bar magnet firmly in a horizontal position.
Touch each nail gently to the magnet and avoid disturbing the stand.
Use separate chains for iron and steel nails.
Pull the topmost nail carefully when removing each chain.
practicals.result: The iron-nail chain collapses immediately, showing that the induced magnetism in iron is temporary. The steel nails remain attached for some time, showing that steel retains induced magnetism longer.

practicals.label: Activity 8.5
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should divide the students into groups and facilitate them to perform this activity.
Take a battery of two cells, a switch, an iron nail, cotton (or plastic) covered copper wire, thread and a few paper clips.
Wind the wire over the iron nail to form a coil. Suspend the coil by means of thread tied to its centre. Connect ends of the wire to the battery through the switch as shown in the figure.
[FIGURE: Coil wound around an iron nail, suspended by a thread and connected in a circuit with a switch and battery; paper clips are shown near one end of the nail. Labels: Thread, Coil, Iron Nail, Clips, Switch, Battery.]
Keeping the switch OFF, bring some paper clips near to one end of the nail. Do they stick to the nail? Now turn the switch ON and again bring the paper clips near to the end of the nail. Do they stick this time? Does the nail behave like a magnet? Yes, the nail has become a magnet. Turn the switch OFF and see what happens to the clips. Do they fall down? What do you conclude from this activity?
An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.
When an electric current passes through the coil of wire, magnetic field is produced inside the coil that magnetizes the iron nail. As we have observed that the magnetic properties of an electromagnet are temporary, therefore, iron object remains a magnet as long as the electric current passes through the coil. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.
If we increase the number of cells in the battery or increase the number of turns of the coil, we will observe that the strength of the magnetic field in each case increases. This will be indicated by the more number of clips held by the nail in these cases.
procedure: Wind the wire over the iron nail to form a coil.
Suspend the coil by means of thread tied to its centre.
Connect the ends of the wire to the battery through the switch.
Keeping the switch OFF, bring some paper clips near to one end of the nail and observe whether they stick to the nail.
Turn the switch ON and again bring the paper clips near to the end of the nail. Observe whether they stick.
Turn the switch OFF and observe what happens to the clips.
practicals.aim: To show that an iron nail becomes a temporary magnet when electric current passes through a coil wound around it.

viva.question: What is an electromagnet?
viva.answer: A magnet produced when electric current passes through a coil of wire around an iron object.

viva.question: What happens to the iron nail when the switch is turned ON?
viva.answer: It becomes magnetized and can attract paper clips.

viva.question: What happens to the nail’s magnetism when the switch is turned OFF?
viva.answer: The nail no longer remains a magnet, so the clips fall.

viva.question: What is the role of the iron nail?
viva.answer: It acts as the iron core that becomes magnetized by the coil’s magnetic field.

viva.question: How can the strength of the electromagnet be increased?
viva.answer: By increasing the number of cells or the number of turns in the coil.

practicals.diagram: Draw a coil wound around an iron nail, suspended by a thread and connected through a switch to a battery, with paper clips near one end of the nail; label Thread, Coil, Iron Nail, Clips, Switch and Battery.
practicals.title: Making an electromagnet
precautions: Keep the switch OFF while setting up the circuit.
Ensure the wire is wound securely around the nail.
Make firm connections between the wire, switch and battery.
Turn the switch OFF when observations are complete to avoid unnecessary heating of the wire.
practicals.result: The iron nail attracts paper clips when current passes through the coil, showing that it becomes a temporary magnet. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.
